source_text: Hoc unitatis sacramentum, hoc vinculum concordiae inseparabiliter cohaerentis ostenditur quando in Evangelio tunica Domini Jesu Christi non dividitur omnino nec scinditur, sed sortientibus de veste Christi quis Christum indueret, integra vestis accipitur, et incorrupta atque indivisa tunica possidetur. Loquitur ac dicit Scriptura divina: De tunica autem, quia de superiore parte non consutilis, sed per totum textilis fuerat, dixerunt ad invicem: Non scindamus illam, sed sortiamur de ea cujus sit. Unitatem illa portabat de superiore parte venientem, id est de coelo et a Patre venientem, quae ab accipiente ac possidente scindi omnino non poterat, sed totam simul et solidam firmitatem inseparabiliter obtinebat. Possidere non potest indumentum Christi qui scindit et dividit Ecclesiam Christi. Contra denique cum, Salomone moriente, regnum ejus et populus scinderetur, Achias propheta Jeroboam regi obvius factus in campo, in duodecim scissuras vestimentum suum discidit dicens: Sume tibi decem scissuras, quia haec dicit Dominus: Ecce scindo regnum de manu Salomonis, et dabo tibi decem sceptra, et duo sceptra erunt ei propter servum meum David et propter Hierusalem civitatem quam elegi ut ponam nomen meum illic. Cum duodecim tribus Israel scinderetur, vestimentum suum propheta Achias discidit. At vero, quia Christi populus non potest scindi, tunica ejus per totum textilis et cohaerens divisa a possidentibus non est. Individua, copulata, connexa ostendit populi nostri, qui Christum induimus, concordiam cohaerentem. Sacramento vestis et signo declaravit Ecclesiae unitatem.
pass_a_gloss: This sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably coherent concord, is shown when in the Gospel the tunic of Lord Jesus Christ is not divided at all, nor torn, but when they cast lots for the garment of Christ, to see who would put on Christ, the whole garment is received, and the intact and undivided tunic is possessed. The divine Scripture speaks and says: Concerning the tunic, however, because it was not sewn from the top part, but was woven throughout, they said to each other: Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to see whose it is. That tunic carried unity coming from the top part, that is, from heaven and from the Father, which could not be torn at all by the one receiving and possessing it, but it obtained the entire and solid firmness inseparably at the same time. The one who tears and divides the Church of Christ cannot possess the garment of Christ. On the contrary, when Solomon was dying, and his kingdom and people were being torn, the prophet Ahijah, having met king Jeroboam in the field, tore his garment into twelve pieces, saying: Take ten pieces for yourself, because the Lord says: Behold, I tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten scepters, and two scepters will be his, because of my servant David, and because of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen to put my name there. When the twelve tribes of Israel were being torn, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But truly, because the people of Christ cannot be torn, his tunic, which was woven throughout and coherent, was not divided by those possessing it. It shows the coherent concord of our people, who put on Christ, as individual, connected, and joined. By the sacrament of the garment and by the sign, it declared the unity of the Church.
pass_b_english: The Gospel reveals this sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably coherent concord, when it tells us that the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ was not divided or torn at all; instead, when the soldiers cast lots for his garment to decide who would put on Christ, the whole garment was received, and the intact and undivided tunic was possessed (John 19:23–24). Divine Scripture says: "Concerning the tunic, however, because it was not sewn from the top but was woven throughout in one piece, they said to one another, 'Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it to see whose it shall be'" (John 19:23–24). That tunic carried a unity that comes from the top part — that is, from heaven and from the Father — a unity that the one receiving and possessing it could not tear apart, but which held the entire and solid firmness inseparably all at once. No one who tears and divides the Church of Christ can possess the garment of Christ. On the contrary, when Solomon was dying and his kingdom and people were being torn apart, the prophet Ahijah met King Jeroboam in the field and tore his own garment into twelve pieces, saying: "Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord: 'Behold, I am tearing the kingdom from the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes, but he shall retain two tribes for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen to put my name there'" (1 Kings 11:29–32). When the twelve tribes of Israel were being torn, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But truly, because the people of Christ cannot be torn, his tunic — woven throughout and coherent — was not divided by those possessing it. It shows the coherent concord of our people, who put on Christ, as individual, connected, and joined. By the sacrament of the garment and by the sign, it declared the unity of the Church.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant content changes and errors not present in the Locked Latin or Pass A. 1. Pass B adds 'the soldiers' (sortientibus is just 'those casting lots'), which is an interpretation/addition. 2. Pass B changes 'ten scepters' (decem sceptra) to 'ten tribes' (decem tribus), which is a factual error relative to the source text. 3. Pass B adds scripture citations (John 19:23–24 and 1 Kings 11:29–32) which, while contextually accurate to the Bible, are not in the Locked Latin source; however, the primary failure is the alteration of 'scepters' to 'tribes'.
reasons: Pass B alters 'decem sceptra' (ten scepters) to 'ten tribes' (decem tribus).
Pass B adds 'the soldiers' to 'sortientibus', which is not in the source text.
